name: Lungfish
label: Dischord
lede: A tattoo artist reciting visions over one riff played until it turns into weather: eleven albums from Baltimore, most of them produced by Ian MacKaye, and not one that sounds like anybody else on the label.

eras.title: Poems over tape loops
eras.text: Lungfish didn't start as a rock band. It started with Daniel Higgs reading poetry in Baltimore while friends built sound collages behind him, and it grew into a band slowly, forty miles up the road from the D.C. scene that would end up releasing everything they made.

years.p: [[Daniel Higgs|6dd4abcc-0321-4ac0-b3bf-0a9422c450d9]] and [[Asa Osborne|4314be59-8f9c-453b-a2bc-7ca086d36a10]] had played together in Reptile House, a Baltimore band that lasted only three or four shows. Wikipedia dates Lungfish's formation to 1987; most sources start the clock in 1988.

years.h: Daniel Higgs' poetry readings become Lungfish
years.p: The tape loops under Daniel Higgs' poems turn into guitar, bass and drums: Asa Osborne, bassist [[John Chriest|4c8b5547-f186-42fd-bc35-47cb13d3030c]], and drummer [[Mitchell Feldstein|769a0231-546e-43e8-bcdd-3a2e13499a37]], Osborne's bandmate from Per Capita.
years.xp: The Baltimore Entertainment Archive lists Reptile House's Gary Breezee as Lungfish's first drummer, with Mitchell Feldstein coming in after him.

years.h: Lungfish's first song on record: Return Descender
years.p: Return Descender, Lungfish's first released recording, turns up on the Merkin Seedy Sampler compilation.
Lungfish record their debut, then Daniel Higgs moves to San Francisco. The tape lands with Simple Machines, the D.C. label that puts it out in partnership with Dischord.
years.xp: Necklace of Heads is the one Lungfish album that wasn't a straight Dischord release. The label later paired it with Talking Songs for Walking on a single CD (Dischord No. 66).

eras.title: Three albums in six days
eras.text: A six-week U.S. tour was enough for Dischord to sign Lungfish, and the band worked fast and cheap: three albums cut in a total of six days, most of their records made down in Arlington, Virginia. Everybody kept a day job. The records kept getting stranger and more hypnotic.

years.h: Lungfish tour the U.S. for six weeks, then sign to Dischord
years.p: When Lungfish get home from six weeks on the road, Dischord Records signs them to make more albums. [[Ian MacKaye|c12f644b-1066-4ead-b0dd-d0c380f5cca2]] goes on to produce most of what they record.

Lungfish's first proper Dischord album, built on repetition, not solos. Bassist John Chriest points to [[Miles Davis|561d854a-6a28-4aa7-8c99-323e6ce46c2a]] and [[John Coltrane|b625448e-bf4a-41c3-a421-72ad46cdb831]] as the model: everybody listening, nobody showing off.

q: If more bands did that they would have less stress
years.p: Lungfish's third album, out a year after Talking Songs for Walking. All three of their albums so far had taken six days of studio time, combined.
years.xp: Asked about working that fast, drummer Mitchell Feldstein recommended it to other bands.

years.p: Bassist John Chriest works at the Golden Temple health food store, drummer Mitchell Feldstein is a licensed social worker, guitarist Asa Osborne moves art for a living, and singer Daniel Higgs is a tattoo artist.

years.h: John Chriest leaves Lungfish; [[Nathan Bell|b00a5223-e0c4-4ffd-90c2-d610b396af53]] takes bass
years.p: After Rainbows from Atoms, Lungfish's bass passes from John Chriest to Nathan Bell, who holds it through the rest of the 1990s.
Lungfish's fourth album, and the first with Nathan Bell on bass after John Chriest's exit.

eras.title: An album a year
eras.text: Lungfish settled into a rhythm as steady as their riffs: a record almost every year, each one another turn of the same slow wheel. Dischord's own description of the band is a continuous quasi-musical pulse that peaked at their shows.

years.p: Lungfish's fifth album starts a run of four albums in four years.
Lungfish's sixth album, a year after Sound in Time.
Lungfish's seventh album, a year after Indivisible.

years.h: Live at the Black Cat, March 28, 1998
yt: Live at the Black Cat, March 28, 1998

years.p: Lungfish's eighth album. By the time it's out, the band is already recording the session later released as A.C.R. 1999.
Six of the ten songs from Lungfish's shelved 1999 A.C.R. session, re-recorded at [[Don Zientara|a495882b-4585-4295-9269-e30c63f279fe]]'s Inner Ear Studios. The other four stay unreleased until 2012.

eras.title: Love is love, then the pulse stops
eras.text: With Sean Meadows, a new bassist from Chattanooga, Lungfish made two last albums, including Love Is Love, which Bandcamp Daily calls perhaps their most magnificent. Then they simply stopped, without anything that looked like an ending.

years.p: Sean Meadows, from Chattanooga, Tennessee, takes over the bass. Lungfish's final line-up is Daniel Higgs, Asa Osborne, Meadows and Mitchell Feldstein.
Lungfish's first album with Sean Meadows on bass. Bandcamp Daily calls it perhaps their most magnificent release.

years.h: Feral Hymns, Lungfish's last album · Dischord No. 147
years.p: Lungfish's final album, and the first made far from home: recorded in California with [[Tim Green|19b6bda7-fbb1-4a45-a3c7-687114167e8c]]. Daniel Higgs later said it best caught what the band actually sounded like.

q: With those two records the quest was over.
years.h: Lungfish end with no farewell, just a Dischord note
years.p: Lungfish never announced an ending. Dischord still describes the band as quasi, if not entirely, defunct.
years.xp:
Daniel Higgs later told The Quietus the quest was over. Daniel Higgs has been blunt about band life: he told The Quietus good music comes out of strife, and the strife gets old. After Feral Hymns he went solo, releasing records on Northern Liberties, Thrill Jockey and Holy Mountain and showing his visual art internationally. Asa Osborne started recording alone as The Zomes.

Wikipedia puts Lungfish's active years at 1988–2006; Dischord's page says about 2005.

eras.title: Solo visions and vault tapes
eras.text: Daniel Higgs became a cult solo artist and Asa Osborne built The Zomes, while Dischord kept the Lungfish catalog alive: vinyl reissues, a radio documentary, and one lost album, A.C.R. 1999, pulled out of the vault.

years.h: Daniel Higgs' first solo album, Ancestral Songs
years.p: The Lungfish singer's first solo record, followed by Metempsychotic Melodies in 2007.

years.h: A rare Daniel Higgs interview, on public radio
years.p: Dischord points fans to a Publicradio.net documentary on Lungfish with a Daniel Higgs interview, which the label calls very rare. It notes the band is inactive and Higgs is booking solo dates in the UK.
Dischord presses Lungfish's 2003 album Love Is Love as an LP.
Lungfish recorded ten songs with Craig Bowen at A.C.R. Studios in Baltimore in 1999, then shelved them. Dischord released the session in 2012 as Dischord No. 174.
years.xp:
The line-up was Daniel Higgs, Asa Osborne, Nathan Bell and Mitchell Feldstein. Six of the songs were re-recorded for Necrophones in 2000; the other four had never been released in any version.

Dischord priced it at $18 on metallic silver vinyl and $10 on CD.

years.p: The Lungfish singer starts Fountainsun, a duo with Fumie Ishii, and also works with the Swedish band [[The Skull Defekts|c4482003-7968-4b29-87ea-bb86c8ffda05]].
Dischord returns Lungfish's 1996 album Sound in Time to vinyl.

eras.title: Still pressing
eras.text: Twenty years after their last recording, Dischord is still pressing Lungfish records.

years.p: Dischord repressed Lungfish's final album, Feral Hymns, on blue vinyl for 2025.
